Response: Thanks very much for your constructive comments. In this revised
version, we carefully reviewed the study by Dansereau et al. (2022) and
incorporated it into the initial dataset of literature review.
For the first comment on the incomplete analysis in our study when comparing
with Dansereau et al (2022), we re-constructed our synthesis to explore the
role of four different hypotheses in driving RUR following your suggestions
and others (i.e. species pool, dispersal limitation, environmental filtering, and
spatial grain size; Lines 52-100). In this case, “the regional species pool size, the
breadth of species richness, and the proportion of rare species” you mentioned were
used to represent species pool in this new version. Specifically, the regional species
pool size was represented by Gamma diversity (i.e. total number of species within
each study). For breadth of species richness, we calculated coefficient of variation
of species richness among different communities (CV_richness) for each
observation, with larger CV_richness indicating wider breadth of species richness
within each observation. The proportion of rare species was defined through dual
criteria corresponding to different data types (i.e. presence-absence (PA) and
abundance (AB); See Section: Quantifications of different hypotheses in
Supplementary Text 5 for details).
As for the spatial extent of the sampling you have pointed out, we found that spatial
extent data were often unavailable in most studies. Moreover, it was challenging to
define the overall spatial extent of the study area for certain study groups (e.g., fish
and freshwater macroinvertebrates), which limited our ability to assess its influence
on RUR (Lines 343-350). Therefore, we alternatively considered the role of
spatial grain size as another important component of spatial scale (See Barton
et al., 2013). It was defined as the sampling area of each study unit within each
study if reported (See Section: Quantifications of different hypotheses in
Supplementary Text 5 for details). We also highlighted that future studies would
benefit from more standardized and explicit definitions of sampling scales,
enabling systematic analyses of scale-dependent RUR patterns using more
extensive and integrative datasets (Lines 353-355).
Our results revealed that species pool and spatial grain size were important
drivers of RUR (See Figures 3-4 in the main text). For species pool, the effect size
of RUR consistently declined with increasing gamma diversity (Figure 3a-b in the
main text; Supplementary Table S8). By contrast, the effect size of RUR increased
with CV_richness and the proportion of rare species (especially in PA data; Figure
3 in the main text; Supplementary Table S8). For spatial grain size, it negatively
affected effect size of RUR although effects were generally weak in both single
factor (Figure 4a-b in the main text, Supplementary Table S8) and full model
analyses (Figure 5a-b in the main text; Supplementary Table S16b).

For the second comment regarding different formats (i.e. linear or nonlinear)
of RUR, we identified linear (first-order) and quadratic (second-order)
models as two predominant forms of RUR characterization through a
systematic review of previous researches (See Appendix 1) and compared these
two formulations across all studies (See section: Effect size of RUR in Methods;
Lines 438-457). Our analysis revealed that 32.1% of records (616 out of 1918)
exhibited significantly better fit with quadratic model than linear model (P < 0.05;
See Appendix 2), while 67.9% (1302 records) showed no statistical difference
between linear and quadratic formulations (i.e. P > 0.05). For these cases, the
differences in AIC or AICc between linear and quadratic models were also less than
2 units, further supporting their statistical equivalence (Burnham & Anderson 2004;
Appendix 2). These results suggested that the linear model provided a more
parsimonious representation of RUR patterns for these 1302 observations (Lines
457-464). Given the challenges in deriving standardized effect sizes for non-linear
(quadratic) relationships of RUR, we restricted subsequent analyses to the 1302
records best represented by linear models to ensure methodological consistency
and comparability across studies (Lines 468-472).

Specific comments
It is not clear if the meta regression aims at testing the “strength” OR “direction” of
the RUR as both terms are used in the introduction (line 39 and line 71 of the
introduction) as well as in the results. There may be different processes affecting the
strength or the direction. These differences are not well explained (but see Dansereau
et al., 2022).
Judging from Figure 4, there would be no association between Rate of species
replacement and RUR if only strength was tested (absolute Fisher Z). But then, Fisher
Z is a metric mostly related to strength (Pearson’s r) rather than direction. This is
a problem.
Response: Thank you for these thoughtful and constructive comments. In the
revised manuscript, we focused on characterizing the overall distribution of RUR
and identifying their ecological drivers. Specifically, we aimed to show the patterns
that significant negative RURs are common while positive RURs are relatively rare
(i.e. we mainly focused on the direction in this study). To avoid ambiguity, we no
longer frame our analyses in terms of testing the “strength” of RUR.
In addition, we agree with your concerns related to the use of species replacement
in explaining RUR in Figure 4 of former manuscript. Therefore, we have removed
this part of the analysis in the manuscript. We alternatively incorporated four
different hypotheses: species pool (i.e. regional species pool size; breadth of
species richness and proportion of rare species), dispersal limitation, environmental
filtering, and spatial grain size in the current manuscript (Lines 52-100). Then, we
mainly explored the effects of these hypotheses in determining RUR and used
Fisher's Z statistics as the effect size of RUR rather than to directly infer strength
per se.
We find that variations of RUR effect sizes are associated with several factors, such
as species pool size (i.e. gamma diversity), breadth of species richness and the
proportion of rare species. The effect sizes of RUR tend to decrease with increasing
gamma diversity, indicating a stronger tendency toward negative associations
(Figure 3a-b in the main text). In contrast, the effect sizes of RUR tend to increase
with higher proportion of rare species, suggesting a potential shift toward more
positive associations (Figure 3e-f in the main text). These clarifications are now
reflected particularly in the discussions (Lines 244-247; Lines 257-259).
It is also not clear why should we expect changes in the strength or direction of the
RUR across taxa and ecosystems. Are factors such as the size of the species pool, the
breadth of the richness gradient, the spatial extent, or the proportion of rare species,
expected to vary across taxa and ecosystems, thus explaining some of the differences?
Probably. These are not detailed.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We did not pursue comparisons of
RUR across ecosystems and taxonomic groups, as RUR is, as you rightly
pointed out, more strongly influenced by factors such as species pool size, the
breadth of species richness, the proportion of rare species, and spatial grain
size. Therefore, we have revised the manuscript to focus on how these factors
influence the overall distribution and variation of RUR effect sizes, both in general
and across different taxonomic groups (Lines 520-564), and have largely removed
comparisons across taxa and ecosystems.
We found significant negative RUR for both PA and AB data (Figure 2 in the main
text). Taxon-specific analyses demonstrated significantly negative RURs
across different taxonomic groups in both PA and AB datasets, such as birds,
terrestrial plants, fishes and terrestrial insects (Supplementary Figure S3; Table
S7). We also found that the drivers of RUR differed by data type: PA-based RURs
were primarily shaped by attributes of species pool such as gamma diversity and
proportion of rare species, while AB-based RURs were more strongly influenced
by dispersal limitation. Environmental filtering and spatial grain size exhibited
relatively weak effects and low contributions (Figures 3-5 in the main text).
More fundamentally, the authors partitioned the LCBD metric (beta diversity) into its
components of species replacement (LCBD_repl) and richness difference (LCBD_rich).
They then tested if the strength and direction of the RUR is affected by LCBD_repl.
First, it is mentioned in the MS that the effect of LCBD_rich was also evaluated (line

LCBD values (LCBD_tot = LCBD_repl + LCBD_rich), there is a high risk of spurious
association here. A full simulation should be conducted to avoid any artifactual findings.

In accordance with your suggestion, we included spatial grain size as an
explanatory variable in our analysis to account for the variation in effect sizes
of RUR. Spatial grain size was defined as the sampling area of each study unit
within each study if reported (Barton et al., 2013; See Section: Quantifications of
different hypotheses in Supplementary Text 5).
We agree that the previous version may not provide detailed descriptions of the
statistical analysis. To address this issue, we have included additional details in the
revised version. For the inclusion of predictors, we explored the effect and
relative importance of four distinct hypotheses on the effect size of RUR. They are:
(1) species pool, (2) dispersal limitation, (3) environmental filtering and (4) spatial
grain size (Lines 52-100). We examined the potential influence of seven predictors
belong to four hypotheses including: (1) gamma diversity, (2) CV_richness, (3)
proportion of rare species, (4) dispersal limitation, (5) Clim PC1, (6) Clim PC2 and
(7) spatial grain size on the effect sizes of RUR across different taxa groups (See
Section: Quantifications of different hypotheses in Supplementary Text 5 for
details). We first conducted single-factor analyses for each predictor. We then
examined relative importance of these hypotheses by conducting a full-model
analyses incorporating different predictors (See Statistical analysis for details,
Lines 520-564).
For the inclusion of random effects, we implemented an inverse-variance-
weighted hierarchical mixed-effects meta-regression model incorporating a multi-
level random effects structure when assessing the overall mean effect size across
data types (PA and AB data). The model specified two independent random
effects to account for potential sources of heterogeneity: (1) nested random
effects of repeated individual RUR estimates within each study and (2) an
independent random effect for taxonomic group to address between-taxa
heterogeneity (Lines 504-509). We also conducted subgroup analyses to examine
RURs across different taxonomic groups. we retained only the nested random
effect (i.e., estimates nested within studies), as taxonomic group was the grouping
variable being analyzed (Lines 510-514).
It should be noted that we conducted single-factor analyses separately for each taxa
group. In these analyses, the nested random effect of estimate within study was
retained whenever applicable. However, for taxa groups where most studies
include only one estimate, we specified random effects at the study level instead
(Lines 535-540).
Regarding the reporting of results, we agree that presenting only P-value is
insufficient. Therefore, in the revised manuscript, we have included the
regression coefficients along with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs),
variance estimates for random effects, marginal R2 values (explained variance
by fixed effects), overall heterogeneity (I²) and the I² values corresponding to

To assess the potential influence of dispersal limitation on RUR, we employed the

Supplementary Text 5 for details). Our results showed that dispersal limitation
exerted significantly negative effects on RUR (Figure 3g-h in the main text;

terrestrial insects (Supplementary Table S12). The same trend persisted after

Figure 3 Variation of the effect sizes of RUR (i.e. Fisher’s Z statistics) with gamma diversity

### Reviewer 2

This new version significantly improves clarity on what was achieved, and because the approach applies more established methodology (e.g., broad search and inclusion of the primary literature, conventional weighting, PRISMA methodology for reporting), it is also easier to assess the robustness of findings. That said, there are still ways to make things more repeatable and clear.
More work needs to be done on how studies were found and selected for synthesis. The goal is to be clear so that the work presented is repeatable; but also that the correlations analyzed is representative of what’s been done. In particular that null and positive correlations were extracted neutrally without bias for negative correlations (publication bias tests help with this, but should be performed among the three databases to assess individual retrieval bias). It is great that the synthesis now includes correlations from primary literature; however, there are gaps on how these new data were retrieved. Given the many authors, how many people were involved in screening studies for inclusion? Was work divided among members, or was there a dual screening design used to improve repeatability of screening decisions? Surely some of the new studies did not explicitly report raw correlations, but presented results as regression coefficients, or slope t-tests, or maybe data were only available in figures. What methods were used to retrieve these more difficult, yet highly relevant correlations? There must have also been some overlap between the different approaches to find correlations—were studies identified in the web of science search that also were found in the figshare database? How were duplicate studies handled? All three PRISMA plots should be merged as a single plot; since the end-product is a combined synthesis of all these sources. Further, given that correlations can originate from three sources (e.g., primary literary, custom databases, etc.), a sensitivity analysis is necessary to assess whether they represent a homogeneous group and that the data can be combined under a single analysis.
The first section of the results is essentially a type of vote-counting where they enumerate the number of significant and non- significant studies (e.g., lines 120 to 122, or parts of Fig. 2). Don’t do this, this undermines the whole purpose of doing a meta-analysis—which carefully does not use significance of each study but rather the magnitude, direction, and sampling error to make inferences. It’s ok to report the composition of the dataset (e.g., number of studies per taxa group, or among categories of responses relative to richness), but not differences in significance. The rank order of effects to emphasize representation of negative effects is ok, but discussing their prevalence without the lens of meta-analysis is dangerous as many studies may be underpowered and visually may not be representative of the underlying (aggregate) effect. Having correlations as Fisher-Z transformed effects is better for clarity since results are analyzed with the metric (e.g., main inferences are derived from these) and consistence helps with understanding what was done in the paper. The results also need to define the acronyms (PA, AB) and more descriptive words should be used for CV_richness, Clim_PC1, and Clim_PC2. Since some details about the methodology are embedded outside the main manuscript, it’s important that they are defined so that the reader knows right-way on how to interpret what was reported. These include the above acronyms, but also measure of % explained (line 176 but explained using different definitions in line 568). Many of the results reported are described as “affects”, for example this “affected” that. If a moderator is being used to explain variation among effects, maybe “predict” is a better inferential description, since correlations are just associations and not causes, and similarly, moderators are predictors and not causes of variability. Finally, lines 517-518 state that significance was tested by 95% overlap, yet there are only p-values reported throughout the results; what is the test statistics these p-values, and their values with degrees of freedom need to be reported along with p-values.
Minor comments:
1) What is the scale of the taxonomic group? Are they Linnean rankings, or homologous groups?
2) Line 194, also 403: “literature studies” should be “primary studies”
3) Line 409: Define what a “unit” is.
4) Line 439: What do you mean by “previous researches”?

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript aims to describe the relationship between, and drivers of, species richness and ecological uniqueness.
Generally, the manuscript reads very well and the comments of reviewer 1 and 3 are well addressed. However, when the quadratic models are tested (as suggested by reviewer 1) and found more appropriate compared to the linear models in 30% of the cases, these records are not considered as the results are harder to interpret. I think that the better fit of the quadratic relationship in such a high percentage of the records show that the relationship can not always be interpreted as linear and that these cases should be considered and not disregarded as the results are harder to interpret. In that way you are only using the results which are convenient, while this is not a good representation of what the data actually shows. Additionally, different drivers of the RURs are tested, following four different hypotheses. In the methods, I recommend a more thorough description of why and how well the variables chosen reflect these particular mechanisms underlying the proposed hypotheses. Generally, I strongly recommend to first run a fully randomised null model, to check if the obtained relationships, and therefore your key results, are obtained by chance or that ecological mechanisms drive this relationship. Lastly, from a traits perspective, beta diversity can be different between sites, but some sites are more ecologically unique then others as the niche and traits of the species differ more compared to the other sites. This is a point which should be considered in the introduction and discussion.

## Paper

## Abstract

Species richness and ecological uniqueness (defined as local contributions of sites to beta diversity of a region) constitute two crucial components of biodiversity. Understanding the relationship between these two components is critical for effective conservation planning, yet global patterns and underlying drivers remain largely controversial. Here, we conduct a comprehensive global meta-analysis to investigate the patterns of the species richness-ecological uniqueness relationship across taxa groups and to evaluate the relative importance of four ecological hypotheses in driving this relationship (i.e. species pool, dispersal limitation, environmental filtering and spatial grain size). We find that negative richness-uniqueness relationships are prevalent across different taxa groups (e.g. terrestrial plants, freshwater macroinvertebrates, birds, and fishes), and such negative association is robust to different data types including presence absence and abundance data. Notably, relationships based on presence-absence data are primarily predicted by species pool attributes (i.e. the proportion of rare species and gamma diversity), whereas abundance-based relationships are more strongly associated with dispersal limitation. In summary, these findings reveal consistent global patterns and mechanistic underpinnings of the richness-uniqueness relationship, offering key insights for biodiversity conservation. We recommend that conservation strategies should prioritize both species-rich and ecologically unique communities to maximize biodiversity protection globally.

---

## Introduction

Understanding spatial patterns of biodiversity at local and regional scales and their applications to biodiversity conservation is a central topic in ecological research1,2. Prioritization in the conservation planning have traditionally been addressed to species-rich regions3,4. However, those areas with high ecological uniqueness—quantified as their local contributions to beta diversity (LCBD) in a region—has recently received increasing attention as a key indicator of biodiversity5. Studies have revealed the importance of ecological uniqueness in conservation planning because sites with high uniqueness may often harbor functionally unique and/or valuable endemic species that contribute to regional biodiversity despite low species richness6,7. Moreover, sites exhibiting high ecological uniqueness may also contribute disproportionately to regional biodiversity by enhancing trait divergence and niche differentiation of specific species assemblages8. As a result, many conservation efforts have simultaneously emphasized species richness and ecological uniqueness in order to better set the biodiversity hotspots9-11. Meanwhile, the relationship between species richness and ecological uniqueness (hereafter RUR) has emerged as an important yet unresolved issue in ecology and conservation biology9-13. Despite perceived importance, the patterns of this relationship and underlying mechanisms have yet to be synthesized at the global scale.

RUR has important direct implications for biodiversity conservation5,13. If species-poor sites tend to exhibit higher ecological uniqueness of species assemblages10,13,14, conserving only species-rich sites may be insufficient. This is because low-richness sites are more likely to contain high proportions of rare or endemic species which may increase variation in community composition (beta diversity) and regional richness—two important considerations in the conservation planning10,11. In contrast, if species-rich sites are also ecologically unique, conservation efforts targeting on these areas may simultaneously capture both species richness and ecological uniqueness13,15. Despite the potential utility of RUR in conservation planning, empirical studies have shown that RUR can be negative10,16,17, positive13,18 or non-significant13. Moreover, the form of RUR may vary (e.g. linear or quadratic10,12,14), and these variations likely carry important implications for biodiversity conservation strategies across distinct regions and taxa groups. However, there remains no consensus on the general patterns of RUR, and the factors underpinning its context-dependency are not well understood.

Four ecological hypotheses have been proposed to explain variations in RUR. First, the species pool hypothesis posits that attributes such as regional species pool size, variation in local species richness (i.e. breadth of richness) and the proportion of rare species may influence RUR through altering the proportion of shared species13,14,19. For instance, if larger species pool size and larger breadth of richness are mainly driven by larger proportion of shared species (lower species turnover), species-rich communities tend to be dominated by common species and show high compositional similarity with others. Therefore, RUR is more likely to be negative due to low uniqueness exhibited in species-rich communities10,16. Conversely, if increased species pool size and breadth of richness reflect enhanced species turnover, this might result in a more positive RUR where species-rich communities are more likely to harbor unique species combinations13,15. In addition, the proportion of rare species has also been suggested to determine whether RUR is negative or positive12,13. An increase in the proportion of rare species is expected to reduce compositional overlap among communities, with species-rich communities more likely to harbor distinct assemblages and become more unique12,16. Therefore, studies have suggested that RUR may shift from negative to positive with increasing proportion of rare species in regional species pool13,15.

Second, the dispersal limitation hypothesis is expected to affect RUR by regulating species sorting in different communities, as weak dispersal capacity of species or strong habitat isolation may restrict them from tracking their preferred habitat conditions20,21. For instance, studies reported that communities with strong dispersal limitation exhibited higher dissimilar compositions than those with low dispersal limitation, resulting in higher ecological uniqueness20. While existing studies have documented the significant influence of dispersal limitation on ecological uniqueness and species richness20,22, current understanding of how dispersal limitation shape the RUR remains critically underexplored.

Third, the environmental filtering hypothesis argues that environmental conditions, especially climatic conditions could influence RUR through shaping species range sizes, richness patterns or species turnover23,24. For example, studies have suggested that climatically distinct regions may select for species adapted to these conditions, which in turn promote small range sizes in those localities16. This may lead to more distinct species assemblage which could shape patterns of both richness and ecological uniqueness. Although accumulating evidence has demonstrated that environmental filtering (e.g., temperature, precipitation) emerge as key determinants of variations in both ecological uniqueness and species richness16,25,26, how RUR varies across environmental gradients remains poorly understood.

Finally, the spatial grain hypothesis suggests that sampling unit size may shape RUR through modulating habitat heterogeneity, community dissimilarity and/or species rarity27. For instance, larger sampling units are more likely to encompass a wider range of microhabitats, increasing habitat heterogeneity and potentially supporting higher species richness22,28. However, this increase in richness may not correspond to increased compositional uniqueness if additional species are already shared across different communities. Therefore, larger grain size may also potentially homogenize species composition across sites and reducing between-site dissimilarity due to compositional averaging29. Moreover, expanding grain size may alter species rarity as larger grain size are more likely to detect rare species that occur in few communities, thereby changing the distributions of uniqueness and richness14,30. Despite its potential importance, the influence of spatial grain size on RUR remains poorly understood and warrants further systematic investigation.

While the aforementioned hypotheses emphasize the roles of different ecological drivers in shaping RUR, they are not mutually exclusive and may jointly determine RUR13,16,25. However, as different hypotheses predict distinct (even opposite) RURs12-14, identifying the main drivers of the RUR across multiple taxa groups is essential for understanding and predicting RUR but remains unresolved at the global scale. Here, we assembled a global dataset combining published and private sources to assess RUR patterns and their main drivers across multiple taxonomic groups (e.g. birds, terrestrial plants, fishes and freshwater macroinvertebrates) spanning broad latitudinal gradients from the tropics to near polar regions (Fig. 1). We calculated RUR using both presence absence (PA) and abundance (AB) data and examined the influence of four ecological hypotheses on RUR across taxa groups. Our goals are to (1) synthesize global patterns in RUR, (2) identify the key factors that shape RUR, and (3) quantify the relative importance of the four hypotheses in explaining variation in RUR. Our meta-analysis provides a comprehensive framework to better understand the mechanisms underlying biodiversity patterns and offers practical insights for conservation prioritization across diverse taxa groups.

---

## Results

The global patterns of RURs

Our meta-analysis revealed a widespread prevalence of negative RURs across the globe (Fig. 2). Meta regression analyses confirmed significant overall negative effect sizes of RURs for both presence absence (PA) and abundance (AB) data (PA: overall effect size of RUR: -0.488, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.583 – -0.392, p < 0.001; AB: overall effect size of RUR: -0.362, 95% CI: -0.458 – -0.265, p < 0.001; Fig. 2; Supplementary Table 1). We also found that the overall effect sizes of RUR were consistently and significantly negative across all three data sources (i.e. primary studies, data repositories and compiled datasets), and no significant differences were found among these data sources either for PA or AB data types (Supplementary Fig. 1; Supplementary Table 2 and 3).

Taxon-specific analyses demonstrated significantly negative effect sizes of RURs across 11 taxonomic groups in both PA and AB datasets (Supplementary Fig. 2; Supplementary Table 4 and 5), including birds, terrestrial plants, fishes, terrestrial insects, freshwater macroinvertebrates, algae, arthropods, invertebrates, zooplankton, reptile and lichens. Several other groups exhibited negative but non-significant RURs (e.g. aquatic plants, bats, mammals, bivalves and seaweed in PA data; Phytoplankton, amphibians, bats and nematodes in AB data). Only a few groups showed weakly positive effect sizes of RURs, such as aquatic plants (overall effect size: 0.074, 95% CI: -0.136 – 0.284) in AB data (Supplementary Fig. 2; Supplementary Table 4 and 5).

Drivers of RUR

The mixed-effect meta-regression models revealed several key drivers of RURs across different taxa groups at the global scale, which were grouped into four hypotheses (i.e. species pool, dispersal limitation, spatial grain size, and environmental filtering). Under the species pool attributes, the effect sizes of RUR (Fisher’s Z statistics) consistently declined with increasing gamma diversity (β = -0.197, Q = 6.81, degree of freedom (df) = 1, p = 0.009; Fig. 3A; Supplementary Table 6), although the relationship was not significant in AB data (β = -0.075, Q = 1.27, df = 1, p = 0.26; Fig. 3B; Supplementary Table 6). Taxon-specific analyses supported these findings, particularly for birds and fishes (Supplementary Table 7). By contrast, the effect sizes of RUR increased significantly with breadth of richness especially in PA data (β = 0.254, Q = 6.12, df = 1, p = 0.013; Fig. 3C; Supplementary Table 6), with similar positive effect observed for terrestrial plants in PA data (Supplementary Table 8). In AB data, however, the effect sizes of RUR did not show significant association with breadth of richness (β = -0.068, Q = 0.26, df = 1, p = 0.61; Fig. 3D; Supplementary Table 6 and 8). Similarly, RUR effect sizes increased significantly with the proportion of rare species in PA data overall (β = 0.400, Q = 8.03, df = 1, p = 0.005; Fig. 3E; Supplementary Table 6), with significant positive association found for birds (β = 0.778, Q = 6.29, df = 1, p = 0.012, PA data; Supplementary Table 9). However, this positive association showed marginal significant in general AB data (β = 0.618, Q = 3.39, df = 1, p = 0.066; Fig. 3F; Supplementary Table 6), and no significant association was found in any taxon-specific AB models (Supplementary Table 9). Most of above results remained robust after controlling for other factors in the multivariate meta-regression analyses, except for breadth of richness with significant negative association in PA data (Supplementary Table 10A and 10B).

Dispersal limitation was significantly negatively associated with the effect sizes of AB-based RUR (β = -0.554, Q = 9.74, df = 1, p = 0.002; Fig. 3H; Supplementary Table 6), particularly for freshwater macroinvertebrates and terrestrial insects (Supplementary Table 11). This pattern remained robust after accounting for other variables in the AB-based full multivariate models (Supplementary Table 10A and 10B). Spatial grain size significantly negatively predicted the effect sizes of RUR (PA data: β = -0.056, Q = 5.82, df = 1, p = 0.016; AB data: β = -0.052, Q = 5.06, df = 1, p = 0.025; Fig. 4A and 4B; Supplementary Table 6), although the negative associations were generally weak in the full model analyses (Supplementary Table 10A and 10B). However, significantly negative associations were observed for birds based on taxon-specific analyses (Supplementary Table 12).

Environmental filtering, captured by the first two principle components (i.e. PC1 and PC2) of climatic variables, generally showed weak associations with the effect sizes of RUR in single-factor analyses (PA data: β = -0.006, Q = 0.23, df = 1, p = 0.63; β = 0.024, Q = 1.60, df = 1, p = 0.21; AB data: β = -0.014, Q = 2.12, df = 1, p = 0.15; β = -0.017, Q = 1.08, df = 1, p = 0.30; Fig. 4C-F; Supplementary Table 6). However, in the full model analyses, PC1 of climatic variables had a significantly positive association with RUR effect sizes in PA data (Fig. 5A; Supplementary Table 10A and 10B). In taxon-specific analyses, PC1 of climatic variables significantly negatively predicted RUR effect sizes for terrestrial insects (β = -0.100, Q = 8.74, df = 1, p = 0.003, AB data; Supplementary Table 13), while PC2 of climatic variables significantly negatively predicted RUR effect sizes for algae (β = -0.044, Q = 4.65, df = 1, p = 0.031, AB data; Supplementary Table 14) and significantly positively predicted RUR effect sizes for fishes (β = 0.102, Q = 3.93, df = 1, p = 0.047, AB data; Supplementary Table 14).

In terms of variance explained for PA data analysis, the full model analysis suggested that 33% of the variation was explained by seven factors (marginal R squared of multiple meta-regression model: 0.33; Fig. 5A; Supplementary Table 10A). Species pool had the largest explanatory power on RUR effect sizes, where gamma diversity (34.5%) and the proportion of rare species (30.6%) were the dominant contributors, followed by breadth of richness (16.4%), while environmental filtering, spatial grain size and dispersal limitation contributed marginally (< 10%; Fig. 5C; Supplementary Table 10B). For AB data, the model explained 25% of the variation (marginal R squared: 0.25; Fig. 5B; Supplementary Table 10A), with dispersal limitation (21.1%), the proportion of rare species (17.7%), gamma diversity (16.8%), and PC1 of climatic variables (16.6%) as the major contributors (Fig. 5D; Supplementary Table 10B). We found higher contribution of spatial grain size in AB model (15.2%) than in PA model (5.9%; Supplementary Table 10B).

Tests of publication bias

We assessed potential publication bias for full dataset (including primary studies, data repositories and compiled datasets) and different data sources. Funnel plots and Egger’s regression tests showed no significant evidence of publication bias (full dataset: PA data: z = -0.13, p = 0.89; AB data: z = 0.14, p = 0.89; Supplementary Fig. 3; primary studies: PA data: z = -0.55, p = 0.58; AB data: z = -1.43, p = 0.15; Supplementary Fig. 4; data repositories: PA data: z = 0.12, p = 0.91; AB data: z = -1.29, p = 0.20; Supplementary Fig. 5; compiled datasets: PA data: z = -1.86, p = 0.06; AB data: z = -0.96, p = 0.34; Supplementary Fig. 6). Rosenthal’s fail-safe values further confirmed low publication bias (PA data of full dataset: 3124252; AB data: 1794882; PA data of primary studies: 97459; AB data: 28703; PA data of data repositories: 1577588; AB data: 1020582; PA data of compiled dataset: 39593; AB data: 25474), all of which far exceeded the recommended threshold for robust and significant meta-analytic results (PA data of the full dataset: 3450; AB data: 3085; PA data of primary studies: 610; AB data: 385; PA data of data repositories: 2500; AB data: 2310; PA data of compiled dataset: 360; AB data: 410).

## Methods

Literature search and data collection

Three distinct approaches were employed here to allow for a broad and representative collection of studies or datasets to be gathered (See Supplementary Note 1: Compiled datasets and Supplementary Data 1 for details):

Peer-reviewed primary studies: First, we searched for peer-reviewed journal articles using the ISI Web of Science using predefined keyword combinations to obtain an extensive collection of primary studies that focused on ecological uniqueness globally. The search was conducted using the ISI Web of Science Core Collection database, accessed via the institutional subscription of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. The structure of keyword combinations was defined as:

TS = (biodiversity OR diversity)
AND
TS = ((ecological uniqueness) OR (taxonomic uniqueness) OR (composition* uniqueness) OR (community uniqueness) OR (local contribution* to beta divers*) OR (LCBD) OR (taxonomic distinctness) OR (unique species composition*) OR (distinct assemblage*) OR (distinct communit*))
AND
TS = ((taxonomic beta divers*) OR (taxonomic composition*) OR (species composition*) OR (species combination*) OR (species assemblage*) OR (community composition*) OR (community assemblage*) OR (community dissimilarit*) OR (community variation*) OR (composition* dissimilarit*))
AND
AB = ((ecological uniqueness) OR (taxonomic uniqueness) OR (composition* uniqueness) OR (community uniqueness) OR (local contribution* to beta divers*) OR (LCBD) OR (taxonomic distinctness))

These used keywords were typical terms in empirical studies related to ecological uniqueness and the last search was done on December 1, 2024. This process was conducted in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement57. Additionally, as a supplementary strategy, we also performed a citation tracking search and investigated all studies that cited Ref 5, on December 1, 2024. This is because this seminal paper provided both the conceptual foundation and terminology of ecological uniqueness (i.e. the metric of local contributions to beta diversity), and which has become a cornerstone in this research domain. Collectively, 1763 records were obtained from these combined search methods (i.e. records of keyword-based searching: 876; records of seminal literature citation tracking: 887) and 1542 records were retained after removing duplicated records (Supplementary Fig. 8).

We established several criteria to exclude several primary studies (Supplementary Fig. 8), these are: (1) We excluded experimental studies because their species combinations are typically artificially manipulated or intentionally set in each community or study unit (Reason 1, 5 studies; Supplementary Fig. 8). (2) We excluded studies that failed to provide taxonomic information at the species level. For instance, several studies limited their taxonomic resolution to the family, subfamily, OTU or other levels, which did not reflect species level richness characteristics (Reason 2, 44 studies; Supplementary Fig. 8). (3) We excluded studies that did not report the distributions of both species richness and ecological uniqueness values, or studies that only report related statistics (e.g. regression coefficients, slope t-tests or model estimates) without providing richness or uniqueness distributions. Although it is methodologically feasible to convert such statistics into correlation coefficients58, this exclusion is necessary because previous empirical evidence demonstrates that the RUR may exhibit either linear or nonlinear (e.g. curve-linear) relationships10,14,25. Without detailed distributions of species richness and ecological uniqueness, we could not reliably characterize the association form of RUR. To empirically test the form of the relationship for each study, it was essential for us to have access to the data distributions. Moreover, relying solely on converted summary statistics would have presupposed a linear association and prevented us from verifying this key assumption. Such incomplete reporting would fundamentally limit our capacity to distinguish between alternative ecological models while introducing substantial uncertainty in the synthesis (Reason 3, 186 studies; Supplementary Fig. 8). (4) We excluded studies that exhibited methodological variation in data acquisition approaches. Specifically, studies combining multiple data sources with inconsistent sampling protocols (e.g., those integrating community data from both literature-compiled records and original field surveys within the same analysis) were excluded to ensure methodological consistency. Furthermore, we also excluded studies lacking standardized sampling protocols, particularly those with inconsistent sampling areas across sampling units. This is because studies have revealed that both species composition and species richness are sensitive to the area of sampling unit30,59. This exclusion criteria was implemented to minimize confounding effects and enhance comparability across studies (Reason 4, 8 studies; Supplementary Fig. 8). (5) We excluded studies that calculated ecological uniqueness metrics based on other analytical units incompatible with our spatial site-based framework. Specifically, studies employing non-spatial compositional units (e.g., temporal observations at different time points, individual organisms from distinct populations, or nodes at food webs) to obtain ecological uniqueness were excluded because these study units fail to capture site-based distributions of ecological uniqueness5. This exclusion criterion ensures conceptual consistency in defining ecological uniqueness as a spatial-community property emerging from β-diversity patterns (Reason 5, 39 studies; Supplementary Fig. 8). (6) We excluded studies that solely reported species richness of specific taxonomic groups (e.g., threatened species, invasive/exotic species, or other preselected categories). This exclusion criterion was implemented because our primary focus lies in understanding RUR at the community or sampling site level (Reason 6, 7 studies; Supplementary Fig. 8). (7) We excluded methodological studies that primarily focused on synthetic/simulated data to quantify species richness or ecological uniqueness, because our analytical framework specifically investigates patterns of ecological uniqueness and species richness derived from empirical observations (Reason 7, 4 studies; Supplementary Fig. 8). (8) We also excluded studies sharing identical datasets (i.e., multiple publications analyzing the same datasets) (Reason 8, 1 study; Supplementary Fig. 8). Using these eight exclusion criteria, 56 studies with 164 unique observations were retained (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Data 1) to evaluate RUR across taxa groups globally.

Moreover, it should be noted that both ecological uniqueness and species richness can be derived from raw species composition data (PA or AB data matrices5). During our literature screening, we identified 44 studies that, while not explicitly addressing ecological uniqueness as their primary focus, contained suitable raw datasets. These spatial datasets satisfied essential quality controls including: (1) being observational rather than manipulated experimental studies, (2) employing consistent sampling protocols across surveyed locations or sites, (3) achieving species-level taxonomic resolution, and (4) containing non-overlapping datasets from distinct research efforts. We extracted and processed these datasets to calculate ecological uniqueness, species richness and RUR. The acquisition of these 44 datasets yielded 124 additional observations. Thus, we retained 100 qualified studies following the PRISMA-guided screening process, which comprised 56 case studies explicitly investigating ecological uniqueness and 44 studies containing compatible observational datasets (See Supplementary Data 1 for details). All retained studies were systematically incorporated into the final datasets, collectively yielding 288 independent observations. A PRISMA diagram summarizing the workflow of literature search is included in Supplementary Fig. 8.

Public data repositories: Second, we compiled several additional raw datasets across different taxonomic groups from data repository, because ecological uniqueness and species richness were both computable from raw species composition datasets5. We separately used the following keywords to search for biological community composition datasets in Dryad digital repository (http://datadryad.org/): (taxonomic composition) OR (species composition) OR (species assemblage) OR (community composition) OR (community assemblage) OR (species abundance) OR (presence absence) (Supplementary Fig. 8). The last search was done on December 15, 2024. These search strings yielded a total of 14693 datasets, 9044 datasets were retained after removing duplicated records across these search strings. We initially screened the titles, abstracts, related references to exclude datasets with unrelated topics. We found that 314 records provided raw datasets of species compositions (Supplementary Fig. 8). After that, we also established five criteria to exclude some of these datasets, in order to ensure the quality of the datasets.

(1) We excluded datasets related to experimental studies because the species combinations are artificially manipulated in each sampling unit (Reason 1, 21 datasets; Supplementary Fig. 8). (2) We excluded datasets that failed to provide taxonomic information at the species level. For instance, several datasets reported richness of taxonomic levels of other types (e.g., genus, family, OTU or ASV), which did not meet the requirement of species-level richness in the analysis. Additionally, we disqualified datasets containing species with missing information (e.g., species that could not be identified or lacked pertinent data within the dataset), as these omissions made it difficult for us calculate species richness (Reason 2, 5 datasets; Supplementary Fig. 8). (3) We excluded datasets that exhibited methodological heterogeneity in data acquisition approaches. For example, some datasets obtained part of their community data from literature sources while other parts were based on field surveys. In addition, we also found that sampling sites differed in their sampling area in certain datasets. Such studies were not included in our synthesis. Meanwhile, datasets lacking details of sampling protocols were also excluded (Reason 3, 30 datasets; Supplementary Fig. 8). (4) We excluded datasets based on other sampling unit incompatible with our spatial-community framework (e.g., temporal observations, individual organisms from distinct populations, or food web nodes) (Reason 4, 4 datasets; Supplementary Fig. 8). (5) We also excluded studies sharing identical datasets (i.e., the same dataset used in primary studies or multiple data publications containing the same datasets) (Reason 5, 11 datasets; Supplementary Fig. 8). Following the established exclusion criteria, we retrieved 243 raw datasets from the Dryad repository, encompassing 20 distinct taxonomic groups (e.g., terrestrial plants, fish, birds, terrestrial insects, invertebrates; Supplementary Table 15). We then calculated ecological uniqueness and species richness based on these datasets. This process generated 1415 unique records of observations which were subsequently incorporated into the final dataset. We have also provided the PRISMA diagram summarizing the workflow of dataset search and the list of these datasets (See Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Data 1 for details).

Following the PRISMA guidelines, two authors independently conducted the literature and dataset screening based on the above exclusion criteria. The two authors examined 3 primary studies and 4 datasets that were only selected by one of the authors. Following a joint re-assessment of the studies and datasets with initial screening discrepancies between the two authors, a full consensus was reached to exclude all of them. We have listed all unselected literature and datasets with the reasons for exclusion (See Supplementary Data 1 for details).

Compiled datasets: Third, we compiled a series of additional raw datasets from our own data. These datasets were mainly acquired through: (1) direct correspondence with principal investigators maintaining unpublished datasets, or (2) using the existing data sources including: GrassPlot60,61, sPlot62 and CESTES63 by ourselves. We included datasets that provided raw data of species abundance (AB) or presence absence (PA). Some of the datasets (i.e. 5 datasets) provided only PA data rather than AB data (See Supplementary Note 1: Compiled datasets). All compiled datasets also underwent rigorous screening against the predefined five-criteria framework originally developed for Dryad dataset selection. In total, 108 datasets with 215 unique observations were assembled and included in the synthesis, 94 datasets of which were published in Ref 43. These datasets include a wide range of taxonomic groups including: Algae (19 datasets), amphibians (2 datasets), aquatic plants (3 datasets), arthropods (9 datasets), bats (2 datasets), birds (10 datasets), fishes (12 datasets), freshwater macroinvertebrates (12 datasets), phytoplankton (11 datasets), terrestrial insects (9 datasets) and terrestrial plants (60 datasets), providing a solid data foundation for the synthesis of RUR (See Supplementary Note 1: Compiled datasets for details).

In summary, our final dataset incorporated a total of 1918 data records from 451 primary studies or datasets (Fig. 1). The final dataset included three types of data sources: Peer-reviewed primary studies (100 studies, 288 data records), public data repositories (243 datasets, 1415 data records) and compiled datasets (108 datasets, 215 data records; Fig. 1). However, for consistency in description, we uniformly referred to each dataset or primary study as a "study" in the subsequent text. For each study, we extracted its geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude), taxonomic group, number of study units (the number of sampling or observation sites). We also recorded the type of data used to calculate ecological uniqueness (i.e., PA or AB data) because abundance weight was proved to be a key factor determining spatial patterns of ecological uniqueness5,16. Additional variables were collected within each study to represent the influence of different hypotheses (See section: Quantification of different hypotheses for details). In general, these studies cover a wide range of taxonomic groups (e.g. terrestrial plants, birds, fishes and freshwater macroinvertebrates) and we divided them into 20 groups (see Supplementary Table 15 for details). The final dataset included 1076 records of PA data and 842 records of AB data.

The calculation of ecological uniqueness

We applied two alternative approaches to calculate ecological uniqueness. Approach 1 was based on total variance in the community dataset5, which the sum of squares from raw species composition matrices (PA or AB data) were calculated and converted into total beta diversity. We then decomposed the total beta diversity into site-specific contributions (i.e. local contributions to beta diversity; defined as Unique_R). Approach 2 involved partitioning a pairwise dissimilarity matrix (e.g., Jaccard or Sørensen) among all study sites, to assess each site’s contribution to overall heterogeneity5,19. This yielded two additional uniqueness indices (Unique_J and Unique_S), based on the decomposition of the Jaccard and Sørensen dissimilarity indices19. The calculation of Unique_R was based on the beta.div function in the “adespatial” package, while the calculations of Unique_J and Unique_S were primarily based on the beta.div.comp and LCBD.comp functions from the same package5,19. All three indices of ecological uniqueness were highly correlated within the same case observations (Pearson’s r > 0.75 for all pairwise comparisons, See Supporting data). Therefore, we prioritized Approach 1 in the subsequent RUR analyses, as it is the most commonly used in studies of ecological uniqueness7,10,12,13,16.

Effect size of RUR

Primary studies have documented different forms of RUR. Through systematic review of previous studies that have reported on the relationship between species richness and ecological uniqueness, we identified linear (first-order) and quadratic (second-order) models as they are predominant forms of RUR characterization (See Appendix 1, which is available on Figshare at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29270048). To determine the optimal form of RUR, we systematically compared these two formulations across all studies. For each RUR observation across studies, we fitted both linear and quadratic models as follows:

Linear model:
Uniqueness ~ β + β *log_richness + ε (1)
0 1

Quadratic model:
Uniqueness ~ β + β * log_richness + β * (log_richness)2 + ε (2)
0 1 2

Where Uniqueness is ecological uniqueness; log_richness is log-transformed species richness to account for its wide range of values across study units in some cases, and ε is the residual error. We evaluated model performance through Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) comparisons. For studies with sample sizes (i.e. number of study units) less than 30, we additionally calculated corrected AIC (AICc) values to account for small-sample bias. We performed statistical model comparisons between linear and quadratic forms using the anova function in R, which performs an F-test to evaluate whether the additional terms in the more complex (quadratic) model significantly improve the fit. Models were considered statistically equivalent when the resulting p-value exceeded the 0.05 significance threshold. Consequently, our analysis revealed that 32.1% of records (615 out of 1918) exhibited significantly better fit with quadratic model than linear model (p < 0.05; See Appendix 3, which is available on Figshare at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29270048), while 67.9% (1303 records) showed no statistical difference between linear and quadratic formulations (i.e. p > 0.05). For these cases, the differences in AIC or AICc between linear and quadratic models were also less than 2 units, further supporting their statistical equivalence64 (See Appendix 3, which is available on Figshare at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29270048). Therefore, we considered the linear model as the most parsimonious representation of RUR patterns for these 1303 observations. For the 615 records where the quadratic model showed a significantly better fit, we examined if these cases were biased toward specific taxonomic groups. We found that quadratic relationships represented 36.1% of PA records and 27.0% of AB records across all taxa groups, with no substantial bias observed across taxonomic groups with more than 10 records (See Supplementary Table 15).

Given the difficulty of deriving standardized effect sizes for non-linear (quadratic) relationships of RUR, and to maintain methodological consistency and cross-study comparability, we restricted subsequent analyses to the 1303 records best represented by linear models. These included of 688 PA data records and 615 AB data records. However, we also performed a qualitative analysis of the nonlinear cases of RUR, better represented by quadratic forms. First, we fitted quadratic models to describe the relationships between ecological uniqueness and species richness in these cases. Then, we calculated the axis of symmetry for each quadratic model and quantified the number of data points distributed on each side of the axis. Based on these patterns, the relationships were categorized as follows: (1) For models with R² greater than 0.1, if all data points were distributed entirely on the left or right side of the axis of symmetry, the relationship is classified as either a "negative association" or "positive association" (i.e., ecological uniqueness decreases or increases with increasing species richness; Supplementary Fig. 9A-D). (2) For models with R² greater than 0.1, if more than 80% of the data points were located on one side of the axis of symmetry, the relationship is classified as a "general negative association" or " general positive association", indicating a predominant but not strictly monotonic trend (Supplementary Fig. 9E-H). We also tested alternative thresholds (e.g., 70% and 90%) and found the results to be similar, and 80% was accordingly selected as the distribution threshold. (3) When fewer than 80% of the data points were located on one side of the axis of symmetry, the relationship was classified as "no general association", indicating that both species-rich and species-poor sites could exhibit high ecological uniqueness. (4) If the model R² is less than 0.1, regardless of the distribution of points relative to the axis of symmetry, the relationship is also classified as "no general association". The details of the distributions of these nonlinear RUR can be found in Appendix 2 (which is available on Figshare at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29270048).

We then used Pearson’s product–moment correlation coefficients (r) to quantify those linearly modelled relationship between species richness and ecological uniqueness (i.e. RUR). We implemented the following calculation strategy: (1) In several cases, the original species composition data were not available, and only the reported values of ecological uniqueness and species richness were accessible. Upon review, we determined that these studies predominantly employed Approach 1 to calculate ecological uniqueness. Therefore, we directly extracted these values and used them to derive the corresponding RUR. (2) For studies providing both diversity distributions (i.e. species richness and ecological uniqueness) and species composition datasets, we preferentially recalculated ecological uniqueness using Approach 1 described above to ensure methodological consistency and then incorporated them into RUR analyses; (3) In cases where studies contained composition data without reporting distributions of ecological uniqueness and species richness, we implemented the same method as (2). Some studies incorporated more than one estimate of RUR in different locations, biological groups or different seasons. Therefore, these r values were included as separate individual observations within each study and then referred to as an estimate. While correlation does not imply causation, the correlation coefficient provides a simple measure of association between species richness and ecological uniqueness, and thus has been used across studies53,65. The Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) from each estimate were then normalized using Fisher’s Z transformation as an effect size of RUR:

Quantifications of different hypotheses

In addition to investigating the global patterns of RUR, we are also interested in exploring the role of four hypotheses with a combination of abiotic and biotic variables (i.e. species pool hypothesis, dispersal limitation hypothesis, environmental filtering hypothesis, and spatial grain hypothesis) in determining RUR. Specifically, to quantify the attributes of species pool, we selected gamma diversity (i.e. total number of species within each study) to represent the size of regional species pool. We then calculated coefficient of variation of species richness among different study units for each observation to represent the breadth of richness, with larger coefficient of variation indicating wider breadth of species richness within each observation. We also investigated the effect of the proportion of rare species within each study, which was defined through dual criteria corresponding to different data types (i.e. PA and AB). For PA data, species detected at less than 10% of sampling units within individual observation were classified as rare. The ratio of these low-frequency species to total number of species was quantified as the proportion of rare species under PA framework. For AB data, we implemented a composite threshold to define the proportion of rare species, and species were designated as rare only if they simultaneously satisfied two conditions: (1) Occurrence in less than 10% of sampling locations, and (2) abundance falling below the 10th percentile rank within the full species abundance distribution. These three metrics provide a multi-dimensional quantification of the species pool hypothesis. Gamma diversity directly measures the size of the regional species pool, representing the total source of potential colonist species available for community assembly34. Breadth of richness specifically reflects the variability of richness within given region - a higher value indicates greater richness variation across sampling units, thereby illustrating how the species pool maintains different community configurations across varying local habitats14. The proportion of rare species reveals the pool's internal structure, with a higher proportion suggesting lower number of shared species or higher species turnover among communities13.

To assess the potential influence of dispersal limitation on RUR, we employed the method of distance-based Moran’s Eigenvector Maps (dbMEM) to model spatial structure across study sites. This is mainly because they effectively detect spatial autocorrelation patterns characteristic of constrained species movement. Dispersal limitation produces a distance-decay relationship in community similarity, where nearby sites tend to share more species (positive spatial autocorrelation). dbMEM variables capture these underlying spatial structures at different scales, from broad-scale gradients to fine-scale patches. This method has been used recently to estimate potential dispersal limitation in various taxa13,66-69. Using georeferenced coordinates from each study (if available), we first constructed a truncated spatial connectivity matrix by retaining pairwise distances below a threshold corresponding to the maximum spanning tree length. Eigen decomposition of this matrix generated orthogonal spatial eigenvectors (i.e. dbMEM variables), with positive eigenvalues representing meaningful multi-scale spatial patterns70-72. We then implemented beta regression models73, employing logit-link functions, to quantify the explanatory power of these spatial eigenvectors, given the bounded nature of ecological uniqueness values (i.e. range from 0–1). The full model structure was specified as:

k
logit(uniqueness) ~ β + ∑β * (dbMEM) + ε
0 i i
i = 1

Where dbMEM are orthogonal spatial eigenvectors derived from truncated distance matrices, each capturing distinct spatial scales of autocorrelation71, k denotes retained eigenvectors with positive eigenvalues, β is the intercept term, β are regression coefficients quantifying the direction and magnitude of spatial eigenvector i's effect on ecological uniqueness in each study or datasets, ε is the residual error. The marginal 𝑅-squared (i.e. Nagelkerke’s pseudo-𝑅2) from these models was interpreted as the potential explanatory capacity of dispersal limitation, representing the proportion of uniqueness variance attributable to spatially structured processes66,72,74. When these variables explain a significant portion of the variation in community composition, the most parsimonious interpretation is that dispersal limitation plays a dominant role in shaping communities.

To assess the effect of environmental filtering, we extracted 19 bioclimatic variables (Bio1-Bio19) from the WorldClim database75 with 30 arc seconds spatial resolution using each study's mean geographic coordinates. This is mainly because of their direct quantification of the critical climatic conditions that determine species' survival and distribution. The species-energy hypothesis posits that climate strongly influences primary productivity, or the total energy available for partitioning within most ecological communities, thereby affecting species richness or species composition via its impact on the number and size of organisms that can be supported76-79. These variables such as the minimum temperature of the coldest month (Bio6) and precipitation of the driest quarter (Bio17) capture the critical extremes of temperature and water availability that often limit species persistence.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was applied to mitigate multicollinearity among these variables. The first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) were retained as synthetic climatic predictors in subsequent analyses (see Supplementary Table 16 for details). We first conducted a single-factor analysis and found that PC1 showed strong negative associations with variables related to mean temperature (e.g., Bio1, Bio5, Bio6, Bio10, Bio11) and annual as well as seasonal precipitation (e.g., Bio12, Bio13, Bio16, Bio19), while displaying positive associations with temperature seasonality (Bio4) and annual temperature range (Bio7) (Supplementary Table 16A). This suggests that PC1 captures a transition from warm, wet, and thermally stable environments to cooler, drier regions characterized by greater temperature fluctuations in general. By contrast, the PC2 represents a shift from warm, seasonally dry climates with high temperature variability to cooler, wetter environments with more evenly distributed precipitation throughout the year (Supplementary Table 16A). We then conducted a full model analysis based on a filtered dataset due to differences in data availability (Supplementary Table 16B). In general, the environmental gradients captured by PC1 and PC2 were similar with the single-factor analysis, i.e. PC1 suggested a gradient from cool and relatively dry climates to warm and wet climates while PC2 from warm and seasonal dry climates to cooler and wetter climates, although the gradient direction of the single-factor and full model analyses was different in some cases (e.g. PA data; Supplementary Table 16A and 16B). Finally, we re-performed PCA on the bioclimatic variables when investigating the effect of environmental filtering on RUR based on single-factor taxon-specific analyses (details of these PCA results can be found in Supplementary Table 16C-J).

As for spatial grain size, it was defined as the sampling area of each study unit within each study if reported. The size of spatial grain not only directly determines the number of species observed and the spatial turnover in species composition, but also potentially alters the influence of other ecological processes such as biotic interactions and environmental heterogeneity27. Larger grains tend to integrate greater habitat heterogeneity and buffer fine-scale stochasticity, while smaller grains better capture local biotic and environmental filtering effects. It should be noted that some studies reported sampling area of smaller sampling units. We converted these values into the corresponding area of the study unit used in the study. For example, plots or transects were divided into smaller quadrats in some surveys, and the area of each quadrat was reported in these studies. In such cases, we summed the areas of the smaller quadrats to obtain the total area of each plot or transect because species richness or ecological uniqueness was calculated at the plot or transect level in these studies. Additionally, for certain taxonomic groups (e.g., algae or freshwater macroinvertebrates), some studies reported sampling unit size based on other metrics (e.g. volume or transect length51). We did not include these cases in the current analyses due to the limited availability of such data. We applied a logarithmic transformation to account for the large variation in the magnitude of spatial grain size. These factors were chosen as they may represent the main potential sources of influence on RUR as proposed by previous studies12-14,16, 20.

Statistical analysis

To assess the overall mean effect size across data types (PA and AB data), we implemented an inverse-variance-weighted hierarchical mixed-effects meta-regression model incorporating a multi-level random effects structure. The model specified two independent random effects to account for potential sources of heterogeneity: (1) nested random effects of repeated individual RUR estimates within each study and (2) an independent random effect for taxonomic group to address between-taxa heterogeneity. We also conducted subgroup analyses to examine RURs across different taxonomic groups. For subgroup analyses by data type, we included both the nested structure and taxonomic group as random effects. For subgroup analyses by taxonomic group, we retained only the nested random effect (i.e., estimates nested within studies), as taxonomic group was the grouping variable being analyzed. The Fisher's Z transformation was used as effect size of RUR, while data type and taxonomic groups were used as moderators in the models respectively. The overall effect size was considered to be significant if the 95% confidence intervals did not overlap zero. We calculated I2 across all effect sizes to estimate total heterogeneity80. We partitioned the total I2 at different levels of random effects set above, to quantify the amount of variation in effect size that could be attributed to differences in between-study, within study or taxonomic groups81.

Prior to the analysis of driving factors, we performed a null model analysis to test whether the observed RURs significantly deviated from those of random communities. The null model randomizes species distributions under specific ecological constraints. For presence absence data, the null model analysis explicitly maintains the incidence frequency of each species, the observed species richness of each site and the total number of species occurrences in the study region. By preserving these fundamental constraints, the model randomizes only the co-distribution of species among sites, thereby simulating communities where composition is driven solely by stochastic colonization under the observed geographic and environmental boundaries. This approach allows for a direct test of whether non-random patterns in species co-occurrence exist beyond what is expected by chance, given the underlying ecological setting82.

For abundance data type, the null model strictly holds two key properties of the original abundance matrix constant: 1. Site-level total abundance: The sum of all individuals in each site/community remains unchanged. 2. Species-level total abundance: The sum of all individuals of each species across all sites/communities remains unchanged. This preserves the overall abundance distribution of the species pool. Meanwhile, the null model randomizes the internal structure of the community matrix. Specifically, it reshuffles the individuals among the sites which indicates that the specific association between a given species and a given site (i.e., how many individuals of a species are found in a particular site) is randomized83,84.

Subsequently, we constructed a null distribution of the RUR by creating 999 randomized null communities. By comparing the observed patterns against the distribution of patterns from these randomized null communities, we can test whether the observed RUR patterns differ significantly from what would be expected by chance. The statistical significance of the observed metric was assessed by calculating a two-tailed p-value. This was done by determining the proportion of null values that were as extreme as, or more extreme than, the observed value. A statistically significant deviation from the null distribution was inferred if the observed value fell outside the range defined by these 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, which corresponds to a p-value of less than 0.05. This indicates that the observed pattern is unlikely to have arisen by random chance, it provides evidence that other ecological processes—such as species interactions, environmental filtering, or dispersal limitation—may actively shape the observed patterns.

Consequently, the null model analysis revealed that a total of 645 records (290 records of presence absence data and 355 records of abundance data) differed significantly from random communities (See Supporting data for details). Therefore, our subsequent analyses examining the predictions of different hypotheses on RUR and their relative importance were conducted exclusively on this subset of records. For these 645 records, we examined the potential influence of seven predictors belong to four hypotheses including: (1) species pool (i.e. gamma diversity, breadth of richness and proportion of rare species); (2) dispersal limitation, (3) environmental filtering (i.e. PC1 and PC2 of climatic variables) and (4) spatial grain size on the effect sizes of RUR across different taxa groups. We first conducted single-factor analyses for each predictor:

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

I have reviewed the MS entitled Meta-analysis reveals widespread negative associations between species richness and ecological uniqueness across the globe.
The MS is generally well written and easy to follow. However, it lacks some important methodological details and coverage of the relevant literature.
General comments
On one hand, I applaud the exercise of evaluating the richness-uniqueness relationship (RUR) on many datasets across ecosystems and taxonomic groups. The main result that the RUR is generally negative is an important one. One the other hand, I believe that the paper makes a poor job of testing the many different processes that could affect the direction and strength of the RUR. Instead, the paper focusses on species replacement (LCBD_repl) as the core process. In particular, the paper fails to revisit the results of Dansereau, Legendre and Poisot (2022), who extensively tested the properties of the LCBD metric on a large dataset of bird communities.
Dansereau, G., Legendre, P. and Poisot, T., 2022. Evaluating ecological uniqueness over broad spatial extents using species distribution modelling. Oikos, 2022(5), p.e09063.
It is clear from Dansereau et al.’s results that the strength and direction of RUR depends on the richness of the species pool, the breadth of the richness gradient across site, the spatial extent of the sampling, as well as the proportion of rare species in the pool (Dansereau et al., 2022). Furthermore, their results clearly show that the canonical RUR is not linear (rather strongly concave), and therefore Pearson’s correlation is perhaps not a proper approximation of its strength and direction.
Specific comments
It is not clear if the meta regression aims at testing the “strength” OR “direction” of the RUR as both terms are used in the introduction (line 39 and line 71 of the introduction) as well as in the results. There may be different processes affecting the strength or the direction. These differences are not well explained (but see Dansereau et al., 2022).
Judging from Figure 4, there would be no association between Rate of species replacement and RUR if only strength was tested (absolute Fisher Z). But then, Fisher Z is a metric mostly related to strength (Pearson’s r) rather than direction. This is a problem.
It is also not clear why should we expect changes in the strength or direction of the RUR across taxa and ecosystems. Are factors such as the size of the species pool, the breadth of the richness gradient, the spatial extent, or the proportion of rare species, expected to vary across taxa and ecosystems, thus explaining some of the differences? Probably. These are not detailed.
More fundamentally, the authors partitioned the LCBD metric (beta diversity) into its components of species replacement (LCBD_repl) and richness difference (LCBD_rich).
They then tested if the strength and direction of the RUR is affected by LCBD_repl. First, it is mentioned in the MS that the effect of LCBD_rich was also evaluated (line 437), but I could not find these results. Second, since both the slope and Pearson’s correlation of the RUR depend on LCBD values, and that LCBD_repl also depends on LCBD values (LCBD_tot = LCBD_repl + LCBD_rich), there is a high risk of spurious association here. A full simulation should be conducted to avoid any artifactual findings.
The above concerns are major, and therefore I cannot recommend the paper for publications.

### Reviewer 2

MAJOR CONCERNS
In its current state, this is not a high-quality meta-analysis and does something I’ve never seen before which is only use snowballing methods to find studies for the synthesis (e.g., screening and including only studies that cite a key paper, here Legendre & Ce Caceres 2013). Typically, this approach is meant to supplement an exhaustive keyword search of multiple databases -- here they skipped the exhaustive search and went straight to screening and including only studies citing Legendre & Ce Caceres (2013). They also supplement sources but do not justify why these sources were chosen or whether they are representative of what’s available. How many studies were missed with these unusual decisions? There is also no information on who screened the studies, or whether there were any practices to validate screening decisions. I suggest the authors have a look at PRISMA guidelines to develop practices that generate high quality syntheses.
They also apply a custom weighting that will have unknown consequences for the meta-analysis and publication bias tests because the variance of Fisher’s Z is meant to strictly model sampling error among effect sizes (and the variability among these weights later, in turn, impact the random-effects estimated by the meta-analysis model), but here they’ve confounded this weight and its purpose with aspects of spatial extent without justification. The meta-analysis model should not be modified like this, and if you believe spatial extent impacts effect sizes then treat it as a continuous predictor in the model, and then explore pooled effects as marginal means corrected by spatial extent. Also please report your full meta-analysis model; it’s unclear what random effects were included, what predictors are combined to achieve synthesis, or whether these were implemented correctly with the metafor R package. Results are also incomplete as they emphasize P values but do not report the statistic of these P values. On Line 131, you also cannot do a meta-analysis of absolute values of effect sizes because this moves the null from zero to an unknown null value -- making significant tests meaningless.
A lot of this work (some of it is quite amazing and remarkable) is simply waste because odd decisions were made that make it impossible to assess the robustness of what was achieved.

3) report the degrees of freedom for all Q tests

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):

straight to screening and including only studies citing Legendre & Ce Caceres (2013).

whether they are representative of what’s available. How many studies were missed
